questions.question: A balance is level. The left pan holds 3 identical bags that each contain the same number of marbles, m, plus 5 loose marbles. The right pan holds 20 loose marbles. Which equation models this balance?
questions.explain: Each bag holds m marbles, so the left pan is 3m + 5 and it balances the 20 on the right: 3m + 5 = 20. The common trap is writing 3m = 20, which quietly takes the 5 off the left pan without taking 5 off the right pan too.

questions.question: A level balance is modelled by the two-step equation 4t + 6 = 26. Which description matches the balance?
options: Left pan: 6 identical tins that each hold t candies, plus 4 loose candies. Right pan: 26 loose candies.
Left pan: 4 identical tins that each hold t candies, plus 6 loose candies. Right pan: 26 loose candies.
Left pan: 4 identical tins that each hold t candies. Right pan: 26 loose candies.
Left pan: 4 identical tins that each hold t candies, plus 26 loose candies. Right pan: 6 loose candies.
questions.explain: The coefficient 4 tells you how many identical tins there are and the constant 6 is the loose candies beside them, all balancing 26. Watch out for swapping the coefficient and the constant, which would give 6 tins and 4 loose candies instead.

questions.question: A level balance has 2 identical jars that each hold j pebbles, plus 9 loose pebbles, on the left pan. The right pan holds 25 loose pebbles. You want the left pan to show only the jars. Which move keeps the balance level?
options: Take 9 pebbles off the left pan only, leaving 2j = 25.
Take 9 pebbles off the left pan and put 9 more pebbles on the right pan, leaving 2j = 34.
Take 9 pebbles off the left pan and 9 pebbles off the right pan, leaving 2j = 16.
Take 2 pebbles off each pan, leaving 2j + 7 = 23.
questions.explain: To clear the constant you must remove 9 from both pans, so 25 becomes 16 and the balance shows 2j = 16. Removing the 9 from the left pan alone tips the balance, because the two pans no longer hold equal amounts.

questions.question: A level balance holds 5 identical boxes that each contain p pencils, plus 6 loose pencils, on the left pan, and 41 loose pencils on the right pan. Sam takes 6 pencils off the left pan and takes nothing off the right pan. What happens?
options: The balance stays level and now models 5p = 41.
The balance stays level and now models 5p = 35.
The balance is no longer level and the left pan drops.
The balance is no longer level: the right pan drops, because the 6 pencils were not taken off both pans.
questions.explain: Taking 6 pencils off one pan only makes that pan lighter, so the heavier right pan drops and the model no longer shows a true equation. To reach 5p = 35 you must take 6 off each pan.

questions.question: An algebra tile model has 4 x-tiles and 7 unit tiles on the left mat and 31 unit tiles on the right mat, and the two mats are equal. Which equation does the model show?
questions.explain: Count the x-tiles for the coefficient and the unit tiles for the constant: 4x + 7 = 31. Do not join 4 and 7 into 11x — an x-tile and a unit tile are different sizes, so they cannot be combined.

questions.question: A bar model shows a whole bar with a total of 34. Directly below it, the same length is split into 5 equal parts that are each labelled n, plus one more part labelled 4. Which equation does the bar model show?
questions.explain: The 5 equal parts give the coefficient and the extra part of 4 is the constant, and together they fill the whole of 34: 5n + 4 = 34. Dropping the 4 while leaving the whole at 34 breaks the model, because the bottom bar would then be shorter than the top one.

questions.question: Which bar model matches the equation 6h + 9 = 45?
options: A whole bar of 45; below it, 6 equal parts each labelled h and nothing more.
A whole bar of 9; below it, 6 equal parts each labelled h and one part labelled 45.
A whole bar of 45; below it, 6 equal parts each labelled h and one more part labelled 9.
A whole bar of 45; below it, 9 equal parts each labelled h and one part labelled 6.
questions.explain: The number on its own, 45, is the whole bar; the coefficient 6 gives the number of equal h parts and the constant 9 is the extra part beside them. Leaving the 9 out but keeping the whole at 45 is the usual slip — it removes an amount from one side of the equation only.

questions.question: Priya buys one reusable water bottle for $12 and several identical pairs of hiking socks that cost $9 each. She spends $57 in total. Using s for the number of pairs of socks, which equation models the purchase?
questions.explain: The repeated cost is the coefficient and the one-time cost is the constant, so 9s + 12 = 57. Writing 9s = 57 throws the $12 away from one side of the equation while the $57 total still includes it.

questions.question: Marcus models 4x + 7 = 31 with algebra tiles: 4 x-tiles and 7 unit tiles on the left mat, 31 unit tiles on the right mat. He takes the 7 unit tiles off the left mat and writes 4x = 31. What is wrong, and what should the model show?
options: He must also take 7 unit tiles off the right mat, so the model shows 4x = 24.
Nothing is wrong — once the 7 unit tiles are gone, the model shows 4x = 31.
He should have added 7 unit tiles to the right mat, so the model shows 4x = 38.
He should have taken 4 unit tiles off each mat, so the model shows 4x = 27.
questions.explain: Whatever leaves one mat must leave the other, so removing 7 unit tiles from both mats gives 4x = 24 and x = 6. Clearing the constant from one mat only is the most common mistake, and you can catch it by checking: 4 × 6 + 7 = 31.

questions.question: Ella's family pays a $30 delivery fee plus $15 for each tree seedling, and the bill is $135. Ella draws a bar model: a whole bar of 135, and below it one part labelled 30 with the rest split into equal $15 parts. How many equal parts are there, and which equation does the bar model show?
options: 9 equal $15 parts, because 135 ÷ 15 = 9; the equation is 15n + 30 = 135.
7 equal $15 parts; the equation is 15n + 30 = 135.
4 equal $30 parts; the equation is 30n + 15 = 135.
9 equal $15 parts; the equation is 15n = 135.
questions.explain: Take the $30 fee out of the whole first: 135 − 30 = 105, and 105 ÷ 15 = 7 equal parts, matching 15n + 30 = 135. Dividing the full $135 by 15 gives 9 because it ignores the fee, which is the same as removing the 30 from one side only.

questions.question: A level balance has 5 identical pouches that each hold the same number of hockey cards, plus 5 loose cards, on the left pan. The right pan holds 30 loose cards. Ravi says each pouch holds 6 cards. Verify his answer.
options: 5 × 6 + 5 = 35 and 30 + 5 = 35, so the pans balance and Ravi is right.
5 × 6 = 30 matches the right pan, so Ravi is right.
5 × 6 + 5 = 35, which is more than the 30 on the right pan, so the pans would not balance; each pouch holds 5 cards.
Each pouch holds 7, because 30 + 5 = 35 and 35 ÷ 5 = 7.
questions.explain: To verify, put the value back into the left pan including the loose cards: 5 × 5 + 5 = 30 balances, but 5 × 6 + 5 = 35 does not. Getting 6 comes from dividing 30 by 5 without first taking the 5 loose cards off both pans.

questions.question: Noah rents a paddleboard at a Vancouver community centre for a $16 flat fee plus $8 for each hour, and he pays $56. He models this with a balance: the left pan holds one $16 block and h identical $8 blocks, and the right pan holds $56. Which move models the situation correctly and gives the number of hours?
options: Take the $16 off the left pan only: 8h = 56, so h = 7 hours.
Take the $16 off the right pan only: 8h + 16 = 40, so h = 3 hours.
The $16 fee is charged for every hour, so 24h = 56 and h is between 2 and 3 hours.
Take $16 off both pans: 8h = 40, so h = 5 hours.
questions.explain: Remove the $16 constant from both pans to keep the balance level: 56 − 16 = 40, so 8h = 40 and h = 5 hours, which checks out since 8 × 5 + 16 = 56. Taking the fee off just one pan leaves an untrue equation, and the flat fee is paid once, not every hour.
